title: Automated Testing
description: Automated tests in Java with JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ and Spring Boot.
resumo: Pyramid: many unit tests, some integration tests, few end-to-end tests.
Every test asserts something; a test without an assertion proves nothing.
Unit tests check one class's public behavior; Mockito replaces its dependencies (`when`, `verify` only when the interaction is the behavior).
Structure: Arrange, Act, Assert — one behavior per test. TDD: red, green, refactor.
`@ParameterizedTest` + `@CsvSource`: one test, many inputs, each reported separately.
AssertJ (`assertThat`) for clear failures; `isEqualByComparingTo` for BigDecimal.
MockMvc is not end-to-end: E2E runs on a random port, or uses Karate.
Coverage shows what ran, not what was checked.

subsections.subtitle: What Are Automated Tests?
subsections.description: Code that checks your code on every build.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** testing by hand after every change is slow, so it gets skipped. Then a change breaks something that used to work, and nobody notices until a user does — and refactoring becomes scary.

**Concept:** an automated test is code that runs your code and checks the result. It runs on every build, protects against regressions, and documents how the code is supposed to behave. In Java the standard is JUnit 5: a method annotated with `@Test` and assertions such as `assertEquals`.

**How it works:** tests run with `./mvnw test` on your machine and in CI on every push. A failing test stops the build before the bug is merged.
examples.interview_question: Why are automated tests essential in agile projects?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A test with no assertion. It runs the code and passes whatever the code returns, so it only proves that nothing threw an exception.

subsections.subtitle: Unit Tests
subsections.description: One class at a time, in milliseconds.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** there is a bug in the discount rule, and finding it means starting the whole application and clicking through three screens.

**Concept:** a unit test checks one unit — a class or a method — in isolation, in milliseconds, without a database or network. Each test checks one behavior, and its name says which. `@DisplayName` gives readable names in reports, and `assertThrows` checks that an error is raised.

**How it works:** test the public behavior of the class: given this input, expect this result or this exception.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between testing a unit and testing the whole system?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Testing private methods or implementation details. The tests break on every refactor even when the behavior is unchanged. Test through the public methods; the private helpers are covered by them.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the service you want to test calls the database and a payment API. If either is down, the test fails even though your logic is right — and it is slow.

**Concept:** a mock is a fake object that replaces a real dependency in a unit test. With Mockito you create the mock, define what its methods return (`when(...).thenReturn(...)`), and check interactions when they matter (`verify`). The class under test gets the mock through its constructor.

**How it works:** mock the dependencies at the boundary — repositories, HTTP clients, message senders — not value objects or the class you are testing.
examples.interview_question: What is mocking, and how does Mockito help unit tests?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Verifying every internal call. The test describes how the code works instead of what it does, so any refactor breaks it. Assert the result, and verify only the interactions that are the behavior itself, such as an email being sent.

subsections.subtitle: Integration Tests
subsections.description: Several components together, with real infrastructure.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every unit test passes, but the query has a typo, the JSON mapping is wrong, or the transaction configuration is broken. Only running the real pieces together shows it.

**Concept:** an integration test checks several components working together, with real infrastructure: the Spring context, a real database, JSON serialization. `@SpringBootTest` starts the whole application; `@DataJpaTest` starts only the persistence layer. Testcontainers (Intermediate level) runs the same database as production in Docker.

**How it works:** keep integration tests for the places where pieces meet — queries, mappings, configuration — and keep the rules in unit tests.
examples.interview_question: When should you use integration tests instead of unit tests?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Tests that depend on data left by other tests. A test passes alone and fails in the full suite, depending on the order. Each test creates its own data and cleans up.

subsections.subtitle: API Tests (End-to-End)
subsections.description: Calling the running application over real HTTP.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you want to know the API works the way a client sees it: a real HTTP request, the full stack, the real JSON.

**Concept:** MockMvc tests the controller without starting an HTTP server — it is an integration test of the web layer, not end-to-end. An end-to-end test starts the application on a real port (`webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT`) and calls it over HTTP with `TestRestTemplate`, RestAssured or Karate, as a client would.

**How it works:** with a random port, `TestRestTemplate` already knows the base URL, so the test only uses paths.
examples.interview_question: How do you test a REST API automatically?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A fixed port such as `localhost:8080` in the test. It fails when the port is busy, and two builds cannot run at the same time. Use a random port and the client that already knows it.

subsections.subtitle: API Tests with Karate
subsections.description: HTTP tests written as readable scenarios.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** API tests in Java need a lot of setup code for each request, and testers who do not write Java cannot follow them.

**Concept:** Karate is an API testing framework where scenarios are written in `.feature` files with the Given/When/Then syntax, without a Java class per request. It understands JSON natively: `match` compares the whole response, and markers such as `#number`, `#string` and `#notnull` cover fields that change on every run, like ids and dates. Unlike MockMvc, Karate calls the API from outside, over HTTP. It runs through JUnit 5, so it is part of `mvn test` and CI.

**How it works:** the base URL comes from `karate-config.js`, so the same scenarios run against any environment.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between testing an API with Karate and with MockMvc?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Scenarios that depend on each other — scenario 2 uses the id created by scenario 1. They fail when run in parallel or alone. Each scenario creates the data it needs.
examples.code:
# WRONG
Scenario: create a customer
  ... * def id = response.id
Scenario: find the customer          # uses id from the previous scenario
  Given path 'customers', id

# RIGHT: create and find in the same scenario (as above),
# or create the data in Background / with a reusable feature

subsections.subtitle: Test Coverage
subsections.description: What the tests run — not what they check.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** how much of the code is tested at all? Without a measure, whole classes can have no tests and nobody knows.

**Concept:** coverage measures which lines (or branches) ran during the tests. JaCoCo generates a report that shows the untested parts, for example an `if` branch that never ran. 80% coverage means 80% of the code ran — not that it was checked, nor that the important scenarios are covered.

**How it works:** use the report to find untested areas, and focus on business rules and error paths rather than the number.
examples.code:
<!-- pom.xml: the plugin only measures with these executions -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.8.12</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>   <!-- instruments the tests -->
    </execution>
    <execution>
      <id>report</id>
      <phase>verify</phase>
      <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>          <!-- target/site/jacoco/index.html -->
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Chasing 100% with tests for getters, setters and generated code. The number goes up, time goes into code that cannot break, and the risky rules are no better tested.

subsections.subtitle: Good Practices: AAA and TDD
subsections.description: A clear structure for tests, and tests that drive the design.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** long tests that mix setup, actions and checks are hard to read, and when one fails nobody knows what it was testing.

**Concept:** AAA structures every test in three parts: Arrange (prepare the scenario), Act (run the behavior, once), Assert (check the result). TDD (Test-Driven Development) writes the test before the code, in a short cycle: red (a failing test), green (the simplest code that passes), refactor (clean up with the tests as a safety net).

**How it works:** TDD makes you decide what the code should do before how, and it tends to produce small, testable classes.
examples.interview_question: How does TDD affect software development?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: One test that checks many unrelated behaviors, with several Acts. When it fails, the name does not say what broke, and the first failure hides the rest. One behavior per test.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the same validation must be checked with ten inputs. Ten copies of the test are noise; a loop hides which case failed.

**Concept:** `@ParameterizedTest` runs one test method once per set of arguments. Sources: `@ValueSource` (single values), `@CsvSource` (rows of values), `@MethodSource` (arguments built in a method). Each case appears separately in the report.

**How it works:** use it whenever a function has many input/output cases — validations, calculations, conversions.
examples.interview_question: When should you use parameterized tests instead of separate tests?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A loop inside one test. The first failing case stops the test, the others never run, and the report does not say which input failed.

subsections.subtitle: The Test Pyramid
subsections.description: How many tests of each kind to write.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a suite made mostly of end-to-end tests takes 40 minutes and fails randomly, so people stop trusting it.

**Concept:** the pyramid recommends many unit tests (fast, cheap, isolated), a moderate number of integration tests (real components such as the database and HTTP), and few end-to-end tests (slow and fragile, but they check the complete flow).

**How it works:** push each check down to the lowest level that can catch it: a rule in a unit test, a query in an integration test, and only the critical flows — such as checkout — end-to-end.
examples.code:
/\        E2E: few, critical flows (e.g. checkout)
   /  \
  /----\      Integration: database, HTTP, messaging
 /      \
/--------\    Unit: business rules, many and fast

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: The inverted pyramid, or "ice-cream cone": many end-to-end and manual tests, few unit tests. Feedback is slow, failures are hard to locate, and the suite is flaky.
examples.code:
WRONG (ice-cream cone):          RIGHT (pyramid):
  manual tests    ██████████        E2E          ██
  E2E             ████████          integration  ██████
  integration     ████              unit         ██████████████
  unit            ██

subsections.subtitle: Expressive Assertions with AssertJ
subsections.description: Tests that read like a specification.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** `assertEquals(true, list.contains(x))` fails with "expected true but was false" — which says nothing about what went wrong.

**Concept:** AssertJ (included in `spring-boot-starter-test`) has a fluent, chainable API with much clearer failure messages. It checks collections, exceptions and objects field by field in a readable way.

**How it works:** start with `assertThat(actual)` and chain the expectation; for exceptions, use `assertThatThrownBy`.
examples.interview_question: What advantage does AssertJ have over assertEquals?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Comparing `BigDecimal` with `equals` (or `assertEquals`). `equals` also compares the scale, so 10.0 and 10.00 are "different". Compare the value.
